title: Palm Nut Cream from Scratch
localName: Banga sauce — palm nut butter, akwu
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: Four kilos of palm nuts boiled fifteen to twenty minutes until the flesh slides off the nut, bruised in a mortar without cracking the kernels, and worked by hand to extract the cream.
longDesc: This is the base of banga, ofe akwu and abak atama, and it is worth knowing how it is actually made rather than only how to open a tin. Palm nuts are boiled until the hard fibrous flesh softens and slides off the nut, bruised in a mortar carefully enough not to crack the kernel inside, then covered with just-boiled water and left a few minutes while the water pulls the essence out and colours itself into a loose sauce. When it is cool enough to handle, you work the nuts and chaff by hand to extract as much thick juice and cream as you can, and strain. Four kilos gives about eight litres.
ingredients: 4 litres water, room temperature — see the note on the two water figures
5 litres just-boiled water, for the extraction
steps: Wash the palm nuts in a sieve or colander to remove dirt, then place them in a large pot with the water.
Bring to the boil, then turn the heat down to medium-low.
Cook 15 to 20 minutes, until the hard, fibrous flesh softens and slides easily off the nut.
In a mortar and pestle, bruise the palm nuts, being careful not to crack the kernel which houses the nuts.
Put the bruised nuts in a large bowl or pot — you may need to work in batches.
Pour the just-boiled water over the nuts and leave a few minutes for the water to pull out the essence of the palm, colouring and flavouring the water till a loose sauce forms.
When the temperature is workable, work the nuts and chaff by hand to extract as much thick juice and cream as you can.
Strain through a sieve and reserve the liquid.
Discard the chaff, and air-dry the nuts for a few days to make the kernels easier to extract.
chefTips: Fifteen to twenty minutes and the cue is tactile: the flesh should slide easily off the nut. Under-boiled and it will not release; over-boiled and you lose flavour to the water.
Bruise, do not crush. Cracking the kernel puts palm kernel — a completely different oil — into your sauce.
The extraction is done by hand and there is no substitute. Working the chaff is what gets the cream out.
Air-dry the spent nuts for a few days and the kernels come out easily. They are palm kernel, used for a different oil entirely.
This is palm nut pulp, not palm oil and not palm kernel oil. One named source is explicit that banga is made with the rich pulp of the palm fruit, not to be confused with palm oil or palm kernel oil.
Four kilos gives about eight litres of sauce. Freeze it in meal-sized portions — it is a long job and worth doing once.
A tinned concentrate is the usual shortcut and is much oilier; decant the excess oil off once it cools and keep it for banga rice.
commonMistakes: Cracking the kernels in the mortar.
Trying to extract the cream with a blender instead of by hand.
Boiling until the nuts fall apart.
Straining while it is too hot to work properly.
Confusing this with palm oil or palm kernel oil.
sources: Adapted from the palm nut butter section of 'Banga Soup: Love in a Claypot', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION: byline prints as 'By Kitchen Butterfly', the site name, not 'Ozoz Sokoh'; credited to the site. Published May 17, 2013, Modified September 22, 2026.
Quantities as printed: 4kg palm nuts; 4 litres water, room temperature. Yield as printed: 'About 8 litres of palm nut sauce.'

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY ON THE PAGE, reported and NOT reconciled: the ingredient list says '4 litres water, room temperature', while method step 7 says 'Pour 5 litres just-boiled water over the nuts'. Both the volume (4 against 5 litres) and the temperature (room against just-boiled) conflict within one recipe. Both figures are carried above under a clear note rather than one being silently chosen. A charitable reading is that the 4 litres is the boiling water and the 5 litres the extraction water, but the page does not say so and that is not asserted here.

The method and cues are as printed, including 'the hard, fibrous flesh softens and slides easily off the nut', 'being careful not to crack the kernel which houses the nuts', and the description of the just-boiled water pulling out 'the essence of the palm, colouring and flavouring the water till a loose sauce forms'.
On what the material is, verbatim from the same page: 'Banga soup is a very special sauce made with the rich pulp of the palm nut fruit, not to be confused with palm oil, or palm kernel oil.'

On the tinned alternative, from the same page: 'The concentrate, is extremely oily so once cool, scoop or decant the excess oil and reserve for Banga rice, a Jollof rice style dish made with the Banga sauce.' The author notes she used canned palm butter for years before returning to fresh nuts.

DISAGREEMENT on the extraction, not reconciled, and one source says the distinction is diagnostic. This recipe pours JUST-BOILED water over the bruised nuts. The Itsekiri National Congress instead says 'Add cold water and squeeze the flesh by hand to extract the cream', and explicitly names cold against hot extraction as what distinguishes the Itsekiri method from the Igbo one (NGA046). Boiling times also differ: 15 to 20 minutes here, 30 minutes in the Itsekiri and Nigerian Food TV accounts.
A useful conversion from Nigerian Food TV: 400 g of canned palm fruit pulp is equivalent to 500 g of fresh palm fruits.

GAP: red palm oil against palm kernel oil is not distinguished by any source consulted. They are different oils from different parts of the same fruit — mesocarp against kernel — with different colour, flavour and fat profiles, and palm kernel oil has its own traditional and non-culinary uses. That gap is recorded rather than papered over.
storage: 5 days refrigerated, 6 months frozen in portions.
reheating: Bring to a simmer. It separates when cold and recombines with heat and stirring.
healthBenefits: Palm nut pulp is exceptionally rich in carotenoids and tocotrienols.
A whole-fruit product rather than a refined oil.
culturalNote: Making palm nut cream from scratch is a half-day job and it is why the tinned concentrate exists. But the fresh version tastes of the fruit in a way the tin does not, and the by-products matter too — the spent nuts dry out to give palm kernel, and the oil decanted off the top of a tin goes into banga rice. Nothing in the palm fruit is wasted.
